title: Software Architecture & Design Patterns
blurb: SOLID principles, the design patterns that actually show up in real codebases, and the judgment to know when NOT to use them.

When NOT to apply a pattern

description: SOLID principles, the design patterns that genuinely recur in production code, clean architecture, and refactoring -- with equal emphasis on knowing when a pattern is overkill.

lessons.title: Why architecture matters
objectives: Explain what 'good architecture' actually buys a team, in concrete terms
Explain how software architecture changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect software architecture with cost of change and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Architecture isn't about following rules for their own sake -- it's about making a codebase cheaper to CHANGE over time. A poorly structured system might work fine on day one, but every new feature gets slower to add, every bug fix risks breaking something unrelated, and onboarding a new engineer takes weeks instead of days.
examples:
# the real question architecture answers:
# NOT: 'does this code work right now?'
# BUT: 'when the requirements change next month (they will), how much of
# this code has to change, and how confident can we be that we didn't break something else?'
commonMistakes: Judging architecture purely by 'does it work today' -- the real test is how the codebase behaves when requirements inevitably shift, not its state at initial launch.
lessons.careerRelevance: This is precisely the lens senior engineers use when reviewing a design proposal or a pull request -- not 'is this clever,' but 'how will this age.'

lessons.title: Coupling & cohesion
objectives: Explain coupling and cohesion, and why you want LOW coupling but HIGH cohesion
Explain how coupling changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect coupling with cohesion and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Coupling measures how much one piece of code depends on the internal details of another -- high coupling means changing one module frequently breaks or requires changing another. Cohesion measures how closely related the responsibilities WITHIN a single module are -- high cohesion means a module does one clear job, not several unrelated ones.
examples:
# recognizing the two independently:
# HIGH coupling: changing the database schema also requires editing the UI code directly
# LOW cohesion: a single 'Utils' class handles date formatting, network calls, AND email sending
# the goal: modules with ONE clear job (high cohesion), that don't reach into each other's internals (low coupling)
commonMistakes: Assuming coupling and cohesion are the same idea -- they're independent properties; a module CAN be low-coupled but still low-cohesion (unrelated responsibilities that just happen not to.
lessons.careerRelevance: Nearly every principle covered later (SRP, dependency inversion, clean architecture) is really just a specific technique for improving coupling and cohesion in a particular situation.

lessons.title: The Single Responsibility Principle
objectives: State the Single Responsibility Principle precisely, and distinguish it from 'a class should be small'
Explain how Single Responsibility Principle changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect Single Responsibility Principle with reason to change and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: The Single Responsibility Principle states that a class should have only ONE reason to change -- not that it should be short, and not that it should do only one literal action.
examples:
# NOT about size -- about REASONS TO CHANGE:
# UserRepository: reason to change = how users are stored (database schema, ORM version)
# UserEmailFormatter: reason to change = how emails are worded/templated
# these are genuinely DIFFERENT reasons -- which is exactly why they belong in separate classes
commonMistakes: Treating SRP as 'keep classes small' -- a class can be small and still violate SRP (if its few lines serve two unrelated purposes), and a class can be somewhat large while still honoring SRP.
lessons.careerRelevance: SRP violations are one of the most commonly cited issues in real code review -- 'this class is doing too many unrelated things' is a direct, practical application of this principle.

lessons.title: The Open/Closed Principle
objectives: Explain what 'open for extension, closed for modification' means with a concrete before/after example
Explain how Open/Closed Principle changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect Open/Closed Principle with polymorphism over conditionals and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: The Open/Closed Principle states that code should be open for EXTENSION (you can add new behavior) but closed for MODIFICATION (you shouldn't need to edit existing, already-tested code to do it).
examples:
# violation: a growing if/elif chain
# def calculate_discount(customer_type, price):
#     if customer_type == 'regular': return price
#     elif customer_type == 'vip': return price*0.9
#     # adding 'employee' means EDITING this existing function again
#
# fix: each customer type is its own class implementing discount() --
# adding 'Employee' means writing a NEW class, touching nothing existing
commonMistakes: Assuming OCP means 'never change any code ever' -- it specifically means new BEHAVIOR shouldn't require editing existing, working logic; genuine bug fixes to that existing logic are a.
lessons.careerRelevance: Long if/elif or switch chains on a type field are one of the most common, recognizable code smells real code reviews flag -- directly tied to this principle.

lessons.title: Liskov Substitution & Interface Segregation
objectives: Explain both principles with the classic Square/Rectangle example and a 'fat interface' example
Explain how Liskov Substitution Principle changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect Liskov Substitution Principle with Interface Segregation Principle and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: The Liskov Substitution Principle says a subclass should be usable anywhere its parent is expected, without breaking correctness -- the classic violation is a Square inheriting from Rectangle but breaking any code that sets width and height independently (since a square can't honor that).
examples:
# LSP violation: Square(Rectangle) breaks code that expects independent width/height setting
# ISP violation: a 'Worker' interface with work(), eat(), sleep() forces a Robot
# implementation to awkwardly implement eat() and sleep(), which make no sense for it
# fix (ISP): split into separate, focused interfaces -- Workable, Eatable, Sleepable
commonMistakes: Forcing an inheritance relationship because it 'seems similar' (like Square/Rectangle) -- similarity isn't the same as a genuine is-a relationship that holds for EVERY operation the parent.
lessons.careerRelevance: This is the same Liskov concept covered in the Distributed Systems course's leader-election lesson (a Square inheriting Rectangle) -- this lesson gives it the fuller, dedicated treatment alongside its sibling principle.
lessons.explain: The Liskov Substitution Principle says a subclass should be usable anywhere its parent is expected, without breaking correctness -- the classic violation is a Square inheriting from Rectangle but breaking any code that sets width and height independently (since a square can't honor that).

lessons.title: Dependency Inversion & dependency injection
objectives: Distinguish the Dependency Inversion Principle (a design idea) from dependency injection (a specific technique that implements it)
Explain how Dependency Inversion Principle changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect Dependency Inversion Principle with dependency injection and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: The Dependency Inversion Principle says high-level code (business logic) shouldn't depend directly on low-level details (a specific database, a specific email provider) -- both should depend on an abstraction (an interface) instead.
examples:
# without DI: class OrderService: def __init__(self): self.db = PostgresDB()  # hard-coded, can't swap
# with DI:    class OrderService: def __init__(self, db): self.db = db  # injected
#             # tests can now pass in a FakeDB() instead of a real PostgresDB()
commonMistakes: Confusing dependency INVERSION (the design principle: depend on abstractions) with dependency INJECTION (the technique: pass dependencies in from outside) -- injection is how you typically.
lessons.careerRelevance: Nearly every popular backend framework (Spring, NestJS, ASP.NET Core) is built around dependency injection specifically because of how much easier it makes testing and swapping implementations.
lessons.explain: The Dependency Inversion Principle says high-level code (business logic) shouldn't depend directly on low-level details (a specific database, a specific email provider) -- both should depend on an abstraction (an interface) instead.
lessons.example:

lessons.title: Strategy & Factory patterns
objectives: Recognize when Strategy or Factory is the right fit, using a real scenario for each
Explain how Strategy pattern changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect Strategy pattern with Factory pattern and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: The Strategy pattern lets you swap an ALGORITHM at runtime by wrapping each variant in its own class implementing a shared interface -- e.g. different discount calculations, different sorting approaches, different payment-processing rules, selected based on context.
examples:
# Strategy: swap the ALGORITHM
# cart.strategy = PercentOff(20)  # or NoDiscount(), or BuyOneGetOne()
# cart.total(100)  # uses whichever strategy is currently set
#
# Factory: centralize OBJECT CREATION
# shape = shape_factory('circle', radius=2)  # caller doesn't need to know it's a Circle class
commonMistakes: Reaching for Strategy or Factory when a simple if/else with 2 stable cases would do -- patterns solve GROWTH and CHANGE problems; applying one to something that will never grow just adds.
lessons.careerRelevance: Strategy and Factory are two of the most commonly recognized, commonly asked-about patterns in real technical interviews, precisely because they show up constantly in real production code.
lessons.explain: The Strategy pattern lets you swap an ALGORITHM at runtime by wrapping each variant in its own class implementing a shared interface -- e.g. different discount calculations, different sorting approaches, different payment-processing rules, selected based on context.

# cart.total(100)  # uses whichever strategy is currently set
#
# Factory: centralize OBJECT CREATION

lessons.title: Observer & Decorator patterns
objectives: Recognize when Observer or Decorator is the right fit, using a real scenario for each
Explain how Observer pattern changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect Observer pattern with Decorator pattern and predict what changes when one assumption changes

lessons.explanation: The Observer pattern lets one object (the subject) notify multiple interested objects (observers) when something happens, without the subject needing to know anything about who's listening -- e.g. a UI element notifying multiple parts of an app when clicked, or a system triggering an event other services react to.
examples:
# Observer: one event, many independent listeners, subject doesn't know who's listening
# subject.notify('order_placed')  # email service, analytics, and inventory ALL react independently
#
# Decorator: add behavior by WRAPPING, not subclassing
# @with_logging
# def process_order(order): ...  # logging added without touching process_order's own code

lessons.title: Adapter & Facade patterns
objectives: Distinguish Adapter (make incompatible interfaces work together) from Facade (simplify a complex interface)
Explain how Adapter pattern changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect Adapter pattern with Facade pattern and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: The Adapter pattern lets two pieces of code with INCOMPATIBLE interfaces work together, by wrapping one so it exposes the interface the other expects -- e.g. a third-party payment library with its own method names, wrapped so your code can call it through your OWN standard payment interface.
examples:
# Adapter: bridge an INCOMPATIBLE interface
# ThirdPartyPayment has charge_customer(amount, token) -- your code expects pay(amount)
# PaymentAdapter.pay(amount) internally calls third_party.charge_customer(amount, self.token)
#
# Facade: SIMPLIFY a complex subsystem
# checkout.complete(cart)  # internally coordinates inventory, payment, shipping, notification --
# calling code only ever sees this one simple method
commonMistakes: Confusing Adapter with Facade because both 'wrap' something -- Adapter exists because two interfaces are INCOMPATIBLE and need bridging; Facade exists because an interface is too COMPLEX and.
lessons.careerRelevance: Adapters show up constantly when integrating third-party libraries or legacy code that doesn't match your codebase's own conventions -- a genuinely common real-world need.

lessons.title: Singleton -- and why it's controversial
objectives: Explain what Singleton guarantees, and articulate the real, specific reasons it's often considered an anti-pattern
Explain how Singleton pattern changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect Singleton pattern with hidden global state and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: The Singleton pattern guarantees a class has exactly ONE instance, globally accessible from anywhere in the code. It's genuinely useful for things like a single shared configuration object or a single connection pool.
examples:
# Singleton: guarantees exactly one instance, globally reachable
# config = AppConfig.get_instance()  # same instance everywhere, anywhere in the codebase
#
# the real critique: this is genuinely hard to unit-test, since a test can't easily
# substitute a fake AppConfig -- code reaches for the SAME global instance no matter what.
# often, passing the config explicitly (dependency injection) solves the same problem more testably.
commonMistakes: Reaching for Singleton by default whenever 'there should only be one of something' -- often, achieving the SAME practical guarantee via dependency injection (create one instance, pass it.
lessons.careerRelevance: Being able to articulate SPECIFIC, concrete reasons Singleton is controversial (not just 'it's bad') is exactly the kind of nuanced judgment senior engineering interviews look for.

lessons.title: Clean architecture & layering
objectives: Explain the core idea behind clean/layered architecture: dependencies point inward, toward business logic
Explain how clean architecture changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect clean architecture with layered architecture and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Clean (or layered, or hexagonal) architecture organizes code so business logic sits at the CENTER, with no dependency on outer layers like the database, the web framework, or the UI -- those outer layers depend ON the business logic, never the reverse.
examples:
# dependency direction is the whole idea:
# Web framework -> Business logic -> Database interface <- Database implementation
# (arrows point TOWARD business logic, never away from it)
# business logic never imports or knows about Flask, Postgres, or React specifically --
# it just knows about its OWN interfaces, which outer layers implement
commonMistakes: Assuming clean architecture means 'more files and more folders' -- the actual test is the DIRECTION dependencies point; adding layers without enforcing that direction doesn't achieve any of.
lessons.careerRelevance: This is precisely why well-architected backend systems can swap databases or add a new API layer (GraphQL alongside REST) without rewriting business logic -- a genuine, valuable payoff of this approach.

lessons.title: Refactoring & code smells
objectives: Recognize the most common named code smells and the refactoring each typically calls for
Explain how code smell changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect code smell with long method and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A code smell is a surface-level sign that a design problem likely exists underneath -- not a bug, but a pattern that USUALLY indicates one.
examples:
# recognizing smells by their SYMPTOM, then applying the matching refactor:
# 'this method is 200 lines and does five different things' -> extract smaller methods
# 'this exact block appears in four places' -> extract shared function/class
# 'this method mostly reads and writes ANOTHER class's fields' -> move it to that class (feature envy)
commonMistakes: Refactoring without any tests in place first -- refactoring is specifically supposed to preserve behavior; without tests confirming that, you can't actually verify the refactor didn't.
lessons.careerRelevance: Code review comments like 'this method is doing too much' or 'this looks duplicated from X' are directly naming the exact smells covered in this lesson.

lessons.title: Architectural styles: monolith, layered, microservices
objectives: Compare monolith and microservices honestly, including microservices' real costs, not just its benefits
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: event-driven architecture, message broker (Kafka/RabbitMQ awareness).
Explain how monolith changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect monolith with microservices and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A monolith is a single deployable unit containing all of an application's functionality -- simpler to develop, test, and deploy initially, but can become harder to scale specific parts independently as it grows.
examples:
# the honest trade-off, not a one-sided pitch:
# monolith: simpler ops, easier local development, harder to scale ONE piece independently
# microservices: independent scaling and deployment, but now every function call that used to
# be free might be a network call -- with everything from the Distributed Systems course now in play
commonMistakes: Assuming microservices are automatically the 'more modern, better' choice -- they solve specific scaling and organizational problems at a real operational cost; many well-run systems are.
lessons.careerRelevance: This exact trade-off (monolith vs microservices, honestly weighed) is one of the most commonly discussed topics in real system-design interviews. These additions were retained because they map to practical software/AI work rather than theory-only study.

lessons.title: Reading and reviewing real code for design
objectives: Practice the specific questions a design-focused code review actually asks
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: load testing, bottleneck analysis.
Explain how design-focused code review changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect design-focused code review with review checklist and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Reviewing code for DESIGN (not just correctness) means asking a specific, repeatable set of questions: does this class have one clear reason to change (SRP)? Would adding a new case require editing this existing logic (OCP)?
examples:
# a genuinely useful design-review checklist, applied while reading real code:
# 1. does this class have ONE clear reason to change?
# 2. would a new case require editing existing, working logic?
# 3. does this depend on a concrete implementation it could depend on an interface instead?
# 4. is there duplicated logic anywhere nearby that should be extracted?
commonMistakes: Reviewing only for correctness ('does this work') and skipping design entirely -- design issues compound over time in ways correctness bugs usually don't; a working-but-poorly-structured.
lessons.careerRelevance: This checklist mirrors almost exactly what a senior engineer's code-review comments look like in practice -- a direct, practical skill for both giving and receiving reviews. These additions were retained because they map to practical software/AI work rather than theory-only study.

lessons.title: When NOT to apply a pattern
objectives: Explain the real cost of unnecessary abstraction, and articulate a rule of thumb for when a pattern is premature
Explain how over-engineering changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect over-engineering with premature abstraction and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Every pattern in this course adds a layer of indirection -- worthwhile when it genuinely reduces future cost, but a real cost (more files, more abstraction to trace through, more to understand) when applied somewhere that will never actually need the flexibility it provides.
examples:
# the honest cost/benefit check before adding a pattern:
# 'I'm adding a Strategy interface for discount calculation' --
# do we have (or clearly will have) MULTIPLE discount strategies? if yes, worth it.
# if there's genuinely only ever going to be one, a plain function is simpler and just as correct.
commonMistakes: Adding a pattern 'in case we need it later' with no concrete evidence that need is coming -- this is precisely the over-engineering this lesson warns against; patterns should follow real.
lessons.careerRelevance: Knowing when to simplify (remove unnecessary abstraction) is just as valued in real engineering as knowing the patterns themselves -- and often more of a signal of genuine seniority.

lessons.title: CQRS & DDD fundamentals
objectives: Explain when separating command/query models or using domain-driven boundaries can clarify a complex system
Explain how CQRS changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect CQRS with DDD and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explain: Domain-Driven Design models software around business concepts and explicit boundaries rather than around database tables alone. CQRS separates write commands from read queries when those models have genuinely different needs.
lessons.example: A payments bounded context might own Account, Transfer, and settlement rules. A command changes transfer state after enforcing invariants; a query model can separately serve a read-optimized transaction-history view.
commonMistakes: Using CQRS or DDD because they sound advanced.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in modern software/backend internship requirements or technical interviews and strengthens transferable engineering fundamentals.

quiz.q: What does good architecture primarily optimize for?
options: Making the codebase cheaper to change over time

quiz.q: What does 'high coupling' mean?
options: One module depends heavily on another's internal details

quiz.q: What does the Single Responsibility Principle actually mean?
options: A class should have only one reason to change
A class should have only one method
A class should never be reused

quiz.q: What does the Open/Closed Principle require?
options: Code should be open for extension but closed for modification

quiz.q: What's the classic Liskov Substitution Principle violation example?
options: A function with too many parameters
Square inheriting from Rectangle, breaking independent width/height setting
Two classes with the same name

quiz.q: What problem does the Interface Segregation Principle address?
options: Clients being forced to depend on methods they don't use

quiz.q: What is the practical difference between Dependency Inversion and dependency injection?
options: They are the exact same thing
Inversion is the design principle; injection is the technique that typically achieves it
Injection is only used in Java

quiz.q: Why does dependency injection make unit testing easier?
options: A fake/mock dependency can be injected instead of a real one
It reduces the number of tests needed
It removes the need for interfaces

quiz.q: When is the Strategy pattern the right fit?
options: When there will only ever be one algorithm
When you need to swap an algorithm/behavior at runtime among multiple implementations
When a class has too many methods

quiz.q: What does the Factory pattern centralize?
options: The logic of deciding which concrete class to instantiate

quiz.q: What does the Observer pattern let a subject do?
options: Notify multiple interested listeners about an event without knowing who they are
Replace its own class at runtime

quiz.q: What does the Decorator pattern avoid?
options: A combinatorial explosion of subclasses for every combination of optional behavior

quiz.q: What's the difference between Adapter and Facade?
options: Adapter bridges incompatible interfaces; Facade simplifies a complex subsystem

quiz.q: What is a genuine, specific criticism of the Singleton pattern?
options: It creates hidden global state that makes unit testing harder

quiz.q: In clean/layered architecture, which direction should dependencies point?
options: Outward, toward the database and UI
Inward, toward business logic -- outer layers depend on the core, not the reverse

quiz.q: What is 'feature envy' a symptom of?
options: A method using another class's data more than its own, suggesting it belongs there instead

quiz.q: Why must refactoring be backed by tests?
options: Refactoring is supposed to preserve behavior, and tests are how you confirm it genuinely didn't change
Tests make refactoring faster to write
Tests replace the need for code review

quiz.q: What is a genuine, non-strawman cost of microservices compared to a monolith?
options: Function calls that used to be simple become network calls, introducing distributed-systems complexity
Microservices are always slower to develop

quiz.q: What does a design-focused code review check that a correctness-only review does not?
options: Whether a class has one clear reason to change, and whether new cases would require editing existing logic
Whether the code uses tabs or spaces

quiz.q: What is a reasonable rule of thumb for when to apply a design pattern?
options: Always apply every pattern you know
Apply it when there's concrete evidence of the variation it addresses, not just speculation about future need
Only apply patterns senior engineers approve
Never apply patterns to new code

exercises.title: Diagnose an SRP violation
exercises.prompt: A class named `UserManager` saves users to a database, sends welcome emails, AND generates PDF reports. Explain which principle this violates and how you'd split it.
exercises.hint: violates SRP -- three unrelated reasons to change (storage, email, PDF generation); split into UserRepository, WelcomeEmailSender, and UserReportGenerator

exercises.title: Spot an Open/Closed violation
exercises.prompt: A function has a long if/elif chain checking `shape_type` to calculate area. A new shape type is being added. What would you refactor toward, and why?
exercises.hint: refactor toward polymorphism -- each shape as its own class implementing area(); adding a new shape means writing a new class, not editing the existing if/elif chain

exercises.title: Identify a Liskov violation
exercises.prompt: A `ReadOnlyList` inherits from `List` but throws an exception on `append()`. Code that works correctly with any `List` (calling append freely) breaks when given a `ReadOnlyList`. What's happening, and what's the real fix?
exercises.hint: a genuine LSP violation -- ReadOnlyList can't honor everything List promises; the real fix is not making ReadOnlyList inherit from List at all (composition or a separate, smaller interface instead)

exercises.title: Fix a fat interface
exercises.prompt: A `Worker` interface requires `work()`, `eat()`, and `sleep()`. A `RobotWorker` class must implement all three, but `eat()` and `sleep()` make no sense for it. What ISP-based fix would you apply?
exercises.hint: split into separate, focused interfaces (e.g. Workable, Eatable, Sleepable); RobotWorker only implements Workable, without being forced into meaningless eat()/sleep() implementations

exercises.title: Apply dependency injection
exercises.prompt: A class hard-codes `self.db = PostgresDB()` inside its constructor. Rewrite this using dependency injection, and explain the specific testing benefit.
exercises.hint: change the constructor to accept db as a parameter (self.db = db); tests can now inject a FakeDB() instead of needing a real Postgres connection

exercises.title: Choose Strategy or Factory
exercises.prompt: You need to (a) select which shipping-cost algorithm applies based on region, and (b) create the correct Shape subclass based on a string name. Which pattern fits each, and why?
exercises.hint: (a) Strategy -- swapping the ALGORITHM used at runtime; (b) Factory -- centralizing which concrete class gets CREATED

exercises.title: Design an Observer scenario
exercises.prompt: When an order is placed, three unrelated things must happen: send a confirmation email, update analytics, and adjust inventory. Design this with the Observer pattern -- what's the subject, and what are the observers?
exercises.hint: the order-placement event is the subject; email sender, analytics tracker, and inventory updater are three independent observers, each notified without the subject needing to know about them specifically

exercises.title: Avoid a Decorator subclass explosion
exercises.prompt: A coffee-ordering system has Coffee, MilkCoffee, SugarCoffee, MilkSugarCoffee, MilkSugarCreamCoffee... explain why this is a problem and how Decorator fixes it.
exercises.hint: this is a combinatorial explosion -- N optional add-ons require up to 2^N subclasses; Decorator fixes it by wrapping a base Coffee with independent decorator layers (MilkDecorator, SugarDecorator) that combine freely without needing a subclass per combination

exercises.title: Distinguish Adapter from Facade
exercises.prompt: You're integrating a third-party payment library with different method names than your codebase uses. Separately, you also want one simple method that coordinates inventory, payment, and shipping for checkout. Which pattern is which?
exercises.hint: the payment-library integration is Adapter (bridging incompatible interfaces); the coordinated checkout method is Facade (simplifying a complex multi-part subsystem)

exercises.title: Critique a Singleton use case
exercises.prompt: A team uses a Singleton for their application's database connection pool, accessed globally throughout the codebase. What's a concrete testing problem this creates, and what alternative would you suggest?
exercises.hint: tests can't easily substitute a fake connection pool, since code reaches for the one global Singleton instance directly; suggest passing the pool explicitly via dependency injection instead

exercises.title: Trace a dependency direction
exercises.prompt: In a clean-architecture design, does the business logic layer import the specific database library (e.g. psycopg2), or does the database layer import an interface defined by the business logic? Explain why.
exercises.hint: the database layer implements an interface DEFINED by the business logic (e.g. an OrderRepository interface); business logic never imports the specific database library directly -- dependencies point inward, toward the business logic

exercises.title: Identify a code smell
exercises.prompt: A method is 220 lines long and handles validation, database saving, email sending, and logging all in one function. Name the smell and the refactor.
exercises.hint: a 'long method' smell (likely also an SRP violation); refactor by extracting each concern (validation, saving, emailing, logging) into its own well-named method or class

exercises.title: Spot feature envy
exercises.prompt: A method on `OrderPrinter` reads five different fields directly from a `Customer` object to format an address, and doesn't use any of OrderPrinter's own data. What smell is this, and where should the logic likely move?
exercises.hint: feature envy -- the method uses Customer's data far more than OrderPrinter's own; the address-formatting logic likely belongs on Customer (or a dedicated AddressFormatter) instead

exercises.title: Weigh monolith vs microservices honestly
exercises.prompt: A 5-person startup with one small product is considering microservices from day one. What would you advise, and why?
exercises.hint: likely advise starting with a monolith -- microservices' operational complexity and distributed-systems costs (network calls, partial failure) usually aren't worth paying at this size; the trade-off makes more sense at larger scale/team size

exercises.title: Run a design-focused review checklist
exercises.prompt: Given a class that both validates user input AND persists it to a database, walk through at least 2 of the design-review checklist questions from this course against it.
exercises.hint: e.g. 'does this have one reason to change?' -- no, validation rules and storage details are two separate reasons; 'is there duplicated logic nearby?' -- worth checking if similar validation exists elsewhere and should be extracted

exercises.title: Recognize premature abstraction
exercises.prompt: A developer adds a Strategy interface with a plugin-style architecture for a discount calculation that will only ever have one implementation, 'in case we need more later.' Evaluate this decision.
exercises.hint: likely premature abstraction (over-engineering) -- with no concrete evidence of multiple real implementations needed, a plain function would be simpler and equally correct; the pattern should follow demonstrated variation, not speculation

exercises.title: Diagnose an Open/Closed AND SRP violation together
exercises.prompt: A `ReportGenerator` class has a `generate(format)` method with an if/elif chain for 'pdf', 'csv', and 'html', and ALSO handles saving the file and emailing it. Identify both violations and propose a fix.
exercises.hint: OCP violation: adding a new format means editing the existing if/elif; SRP violation: format generation, saving, and emailing are three separate reasons to change. Fix: separate format-specific generator classes (OCP), plus separate FileSaver and EmailSender classes (SRP)

exercises.title: Choose composition over inheritance for a DI-friendly design
exercises.prompt: Design a `NotificationService` that can send via email OR SMS, decided at construction time, and is easy to unit test. Sketch the class relationships (in words, not code) using concepts from this course.
exercises.hint: use dependency injection: NotificationService accepts a Sender interface (Strategy pattern) in its constructor; EmailSender and SMSSender each implement Sender; tests inject a FakeSender to verify behavior without real email/SMS calls

projects.title: Refactor a God class
projects.desc: Given a single class handling validation, storage, and notification, split it into focused classes honoring SRP, with tests proving behavior is unchanged.

projects.title: Build a pluggable discount system with Strategy
projects.desc: Design a discount system supporting at least 3 real strategies, added without modifying the existing checkout code (Open/Closed in practice).

projects.title: Add dependency injection to a hard-coded design
projects.desc: Take a class with hard-coded dependencies (database, email service) and refactor it to accept them via constructor injection, with tests using fake implementations.

projects.title: Design a Facade over a multi-step checkout process
projects.desc: Build a simple Facade coordinating inventory, payment, and shipping subsystems behind one clean method.

projects.title: Write a design-focused code review
projects.desc: Given a real-shaped code sample with multiple design issues, write a structured review identifying at least 3 concrete violations and proposing specific fixes for each.

interviewPreparation.q: Explain the Single Responsibility Principle with a concrete example, not just the definition.
interviewPreparation.a: A class should have only one reason to change. For example, a class that both saves a user to a database AND formats a user for an email has two separate reasons to change: a storage-format change, or an email-template change. These should be split into two focused classes so each concern can change independently without touching the other.

interviewPreparation.q: What's the practical difference between Dependency Inversion and dependency injection?
interviewPreparation.a: Dependency Inversion is the design principle: high-level code should depend on abstractions, not concrete low-level details. Dependency injection is the specific technique that typically achieves this: instead of a class creating its own dependency internally, the dependency is passed in from outside, allowing real or fake implementations to be swapped in -- which is exactly why DI makes unit testing significantly easier.

interviewPreparation.q: When would you choose Strategy over a simple if/else, and when would the if/else actually be the better choice?
interviewPreparation.a: Strategy is worth the extra indirection when there are multiple real (or near-certain future) variations of a behavior that need to be swapped independently. If there are only two stable cases that will essentially never grow, a simple if/else is simpler and just as correct -- adding Strategy there would be premature abstraction with no real payoff.

interviewPreparation.q: What are the genuine, specific costs of microservices compared to a monolith -- not just the commonly cited benefits?
interviewPreparation.a: Function calls that used to be simple, reliable in-process calls become network calls, introducing real distributed-systems complexity: partial failure, retries, timeouts, and consistency concerns. Microservices also add significant operational overhead -- more deployments to manage, more services to monitor, more points of failure. These are genuine costs, not just complexity for complexity's sake, which is why many successful systems remain monoliths.

interviewPreparation.q: Why is Singleton often considered an anti-pattern despite being useful?
interviewPreparation.a: It creates hidden global state that any code, anywhere, can read or modify, making behavior harder to reason about. It also makes unit testing meaningfully harder, since tests can't easily substitute a fake instance -- code reaches for the same global Singleton directly. Often, achieving the same 'exactly one instance' guarantee via dependency injection (creating one instance and passing it explicitly) provides the same benefit without these specific costs.

capstone.title: Refactor a Poorly Designed System, With Evidence
capstone.description: Given (or designing your own) a small system with multiple real design violations -- SRP, OCP, tight coupling, hard-coded dependencies -- identify each violation explicitly, apply the appropriate principle or pattern to fix it, and prove with tests that behavior didn't change during the refactor.
deliverables: A written list of at least 4 specific design violations found, each naming the principle or smell it violates
The refactored code applying an appropriate fix for each violation (e.g. splitting an SRP-violating class, introducing dependency injection, replacing an if/elif chain with Strategy or polymorphism)
A test suite proving the refactored code behaves identically to the original for the same inputs
A short written justification for each pattern used -- specifically citing the concrete evidence of variation or coupling that justified it, not just 'this seemed like a good pattern to use'
At least one explicit note about a place you deliberately did NOT apply a pattern, and why the simpler approach was the right call there
capstone.portfolioTips: That last deliverable -- explicitly justifying where you did NOT add abstraction -- is exactly the kind of judgment that distinguishes a strong architecture portfolio piece from one that just lists patterns applied for their own sake.

industryUsage.usage: Both frameworks are built entirely around dependency injection as a first-class feature, specifically because of how much easier it makes testing and swapping implementations at scale.

Both are frequently cited examples of large-scale microservices architectures -- and both have also publicly discussed the real operational complexity that came with that choice, illustrating the honest trade-off covered in this course.

The SOLID principles and named code smells in this course are the direct, everyday vocabulary used in real pull-request review comments across the industry -- 'this violates SRP' or 'this looks like feature envy' are genuine, common review feedback, not just textbook terms.

careerApplications: Used by senior software engineers and technical leads to define service boundaries, interfaces, data flow, failure behavior, scalability, maintainability, and trade-offs before large implementations.
